goldenRule.mantra: SLOW APPROACH → FAST → POWER STEP → CLOSING → VERTICAL JUMP → ARM EXTENDED FORWARD → WRIST SNAP
goldenRule.body: Power comes from the full kinetic chain, not the arm alone. A well-timed approach with fast last two steps generates 70% of final power.

phases.title: The 5 phases of the spike

items.name: Initiation
items.desc: Reading the set and deciding on the approach

items.name: Wind-up
items.desc: Start of the approach

items.name: Cocking
items.desc: Elbow above the shoulder, hand behind the ear — power position

items.name: Acceleration
items.desc: Sequential rotation: hips → torso → shoulder → elbow → wrist

items.name: Contact + follow-through
items.desc: Wrist snap, the hand "claws" over the top of the ball → topspin

phases.footer: Slightly in front of the hitting shoulder, never behind the head (power loss + injury risk). Distance to the net at takeoff: 30-50 cm minimum.

items.label: Step 1 (left)
items.text: Short directional step, oriented toward the attack

items.label: Step 2 (right)
items.text: Power step — long and low, heel first, center of gravity drops

items.label: Step 3 (left)
items.text: Closing step — short, brakes horizontal momentum and converts it into vertical

four.title: 4 steps — Competition standard

items.label: Step 1 (right)
items.text: Observation step, slow tempo

items.label: Step 2 (left)
items.text: Acceleration

items.label: Step 3 (right)
items.text: Power step — the most important, long and low

items.label: Step 4 (left)
items.text: Closing step parallel to the net

four.rule: Golden rule: the last two steps are the fastest — slow → fast.

rows.timing: Start LATE — when the ball leaves the setter's hands
Start when the pass is on its way to the setter
Start EARLY — already in the air when the setter touches the ball
Start the moment the setter receives the pass

items.name: Zone 4 attack (Outside / OH)
items.description: The foundation of learning to attack. The outside hitter receives the largest volume of sets — the setter's "safety" option. Approach at 45° from the left.
keyPoints: 4-step approach at ~45° relative to the net
Jump VERTICALLY — not toward the net
Contact slightly in front of the hitting shoulder

items.name: Middle attack (Quick / 1st tempo)
items.description: The fastest attack. The middle is in the air BEFORE or as the setter touches the ball. Very low (30-50 cm) and very short set.
keyPoints: Trigger the approach EARLY — already in the air when the setter releases
2-3 step approach, arm already loaded on the way up
"Ghost Middle" concept: even if the ball doesn't come, run the quick full speed to fix the opposing block → frees the outsides
Fast transition: block → approach in 1-2 seconds

items.name: Zone 2 attack (Opposite)
items.description: The opposite attacks from zone 2. Ideal for left-handers (hitting shoulder on the right antenna side = maximum hitting window). For right-handers: more pronounced torso rotation, position farther from the antenna.
keyPoints: Approach symmetrical to the outside hitter but from the right
Finish with thumb down for the cut shot
Setter's "release" option when the reception is broken
Back-row attack from P1 (zone D) when in back row

items.name: Back-row attack (Pipe)
items.description: Attack from the back row. The plant MUST happen BEHIND the 3 m line. Allows 4 attackers against 3 blockers.
keyPoints: Takeoff mandatory behind the 3 m line (otherwise a fault)
Landing in the front zone after a legal jump is OK
Pipe: from P6, set above the quick (BIC = just above the quick)
Zone D: from P1, often the opposite's safety attack

items.name: Tip
items.desc: IDENTICAL approach to the spike (disguise is crucial), then at contact slow the arm and place the ball with a fingertip touch. Direction: empty zone identified BEFORE the jump.

items.name: Roll shot / topspin off-speed
items.desc: Reduced-speed contact (~50-70%) with heavy topspin so the ball drops short behind the block. Harder to read than the tip because it's faster.

items.name: Cut shot / sharp angle
items.desc: Sharp angle toward zone 1 (from 4) or zone 5 (from 2). Finish with thumb down, hand cutting laterally across the ball. Hit the side of the ball, not the top.

items.name: Tooling / Wipe
items.desc: Intentionally push the ball out off the block. On a tight set, jump vertically and push the ball laterally using the blocker's outside hand as a "rail".

items.label: Approach timing
items.text: Too early: powerless re-jump. Too late: arm extended behind you at contact.

items.label: Wrong foot order
items.text: Always finish on left-right (right-handed) — both feet nearly simultaneous.

items.label: No topspin
items.text: Flat hand = no snap = ball sails long. "Claw" over the top of the ball.

items.label: Net fault
items.text: Jumping forward on a tight set. Jump VERTICALLY, not forward.

items.label: Back-row fault
items.text: Foot on or in front of the 3 m line at takeoff.

items.label: One-foot landing
items.text: Except for the slide: land on both feet to protect the knee (ACL risk).

goldenRule.mantra: BALL → SETTER → BALL → HITTER'S SHOULDER → JUMP → PENETRATION
goldenRule.body: With regular practice and special attention to timing, you'll dramatically improve your blocks. A well-timed block with moderate jump height beats a very high jump that's poorly timed.

fundamentals.title: The fundamentals of blocking
fundamentals.html: The block is a crucial defensive skill that can become an offensive weapon. The key lies in perfect timing and good reading of the play.

items.title: Watch the hitter, not the ball
items.desc: Watch the hitter's shoulders and arm to anticipate the moment and direction of the strike.

items.title: Jump AFTER the hitter
items.desc: Wait until the hitter is in their takeoff phase. If you jump at the same time or earlier, you'll come down too early.

items.title: The ideal delay: 0.2 to 0.3 seconds
items.desc: Mentally count "ONE" when the hitter jumps, then jump immediately after. That fraction of a second is crucial.

items.title: Penetrate over the net
items.desc: At the peak of your jump, push your hands and arms forward and downward — not just upward.

items.name: The offensive block
items.objective: Send the ball directly back into the opponent's court

points.label: Position
points.text: Hands spread, fingers extended and spread

points.label: Action
points.text: Penetrate as far as possible over the net, arms extended forward

points.label: Target
points.text: Brace your wrists to drive the ball down into the opponent's floor

points.label: When
points.text: When you're well placed and have read the attack

items.name: The soft block (cover block)
items.objective: Slow the ball down so your defense can recover

points.label: Position
points.text: Hands close together, palms angled toward you

points.label: Action
points.text: Absorb the impact rather than push

points.label: Result
points.text: The ball falls softly into your court to be played

points.label: When
points.text: When you're late or out of position

points.label: Position
points.text: Block a specific area (line or cross-court)

points.label: Action
points.text: Orient your hands toward the area you want to protect

points.label: Tactic
points.text: Force the hitter to swing into a zone where your defenders are ready

points.label: Coordination
points.text: Jump together at the same moment

points.label: Placement
points.text: Outside blockers position themselves based on the middle blocker

points.label: Hands
points.text: Join your hands with your teammates' (no gaps)

points.label: Communication
points.text: One blocker calls "line" or "cross" to coordinate

items.label: The "one-two" drill
items.text: In practice, say "ONE" when the hitter jumps, "TWO" when you jump. It builds the necessary delay.

items.label: Watch the shoulders
items.text: The hitter's shoulder orientation tells you the direction of the strike.

items.label: Analyze the set
items.text: A high set = more time. A low set = quick reaction.

items.label: Get into position early
items.text: Better to wait in position than to run there at the last second.

items.label: Work on your vertical
items.text: The higher you jump, the more margin for error on timing.

visualSequence.title: Elite visual sequence
visualSequence.intro: The best blockers don't watch the ball — they follow a precise sequence:

items.label: 1. BALL
items.text: See the ball heading toward the setter

items.label: 2. SETTER
items.text: Read the setter's hands at the moment of contact — direction of the set

items.label: 3. BALL
items.text: Briefly track the ball to confirm direction

items.label: 4. HITTER'S SHOULDER
items.text: Lock onto the hitter's shoulder — it gives you the direction of the strike before contact

rows.timing: WITH or a hair before the hitter (commit block)
WITH or just after — track laterally

read.label: Read blocking — recommended
read.body: The blocker waits for the setter's decision, reads the ball and the hitter, then moves. "Bunch read" position (all close to the middle, then explode to the pin).
points: Stable and present on the majority of sets

commit.label: Commit blocking — advanced/pro
commit.body: The middle decides BEFORE the setter releases to jump with the quick. Eliminates the opponent's quick attack, but if the setter sets elsewhere, the middle is completely out of the play.
points: High risk if the setter adjusts
Reserved for players with excellent reading

items.text: Feet shoulder-width apart
Weight on the balls of the feet
Knees slightly bent
Arms along the body or slightly in front
Stand about 30–50 cm from the net

items.label: Shuffle step
items.text: If you need to move, use a fast shuffle step

items.label: Load
items.text: Bend your legs quickly (don't drop too low)

items.label: Arm swing
items.text: Throw your arms upward explosively

items.label: Full extension
items.text: Fully extend your legs to maximize height
Keep your arms extended and tight
Hands spread, fingers extended and spread
Penetrate over the net (no net touch!)
Brace your core to stay stable

items.label: Jumping too early
items.text: You're coming down as the hitter swings — wait longer!

items.label: Watching the ball
items.text: You miss information on the hitter — watch the player!

items.label: Soft hands
items.text: The ball bounces back into your court — extend and tense your fingers!

items.label: Jumping forward
items.text: You touch the net — jump vertically!

items.label: Lowering arms too early
items.text: Keep your arms up until you land.

items.title: Partner timing
items.desc: A partner fakes an attack (no ball). You work only on your jump timing. Repeat 20 times.

items.title: Block on fixed attack
items.desc: A hitter swings from a fixed position. Focus on timing and technique. Gradually increase speed.

items.title: Shoulder reading
items.desc: The hitter varies their swings (line/cross). Try to read their shoulders to anticipate direction.

items.title: Footwork + block
items.desc: Work on fast lateral footwork followed by a block. Simulates match situations.

items.label: Patience
items.text: Blocking is one of the hardest skills. Be patient with yourself.

items.label: Repetition
items.text: Muscle memory is built through hundreds of reps.

items.label: Video
items.text: Film yourself to analyze your timing and technique.

items.label: Watch the pros
items.text: Watch how professional players read the game and time their jumps.

items.label: Start simple
items.text: Master blocking slow attacks before moving on to fast ones.

goldenRule.body: 80% of serving errors come from the toss. Stabilize the toss first, before chasing power.

items.name: Underhand serve
items.description: Pendulum motion of the hitting arm below the waist. Legal at every level, recommended for beginners or in case of a shoulder injury. Almost nonexistent above adult regional level.
biomechanics: Short kinetic chain: hips → shoulder → arm → hand
Pendulum motion without torso rotation
Weight transfer: back foot → front foot
Contact: heel of the hand or closed fist beneath the center of the ball
steps: Left foot forward, weight on the back leg
Left hand holds the ball at hip height, aligned with the arm
Right arm cocked back, palm open or fist closed
Release the ball just before contact — don't toss it
Swing forward, strike below the center of the ball
Arm follows through and points at the target, weight transferred to the front foot

errors.label: Ball held too low or off to the side
errors.text: Keep the ball at hip height, aligned with the hitting arm

errors.label: Striking with the fingers
errors.text: Use the heel of the hand — broader, more stable surface

errors.label: Tossing too high
errors.text: Just release the ball, don't toss it up

errors.label: Soft wrist
errors.text: Lock the arm at contact for a clean impact

exercises: Hoops bowling: aim at zones 4 m from the net
10 serves from 4 m, then back up 1 m per set until the end line
4×3 m floor targets — aim for 50% accuracy

items.name: Standing float serve
items.tagline: standing float — the default serve for 90% of amateurs
items.description: A serve with no rotation that produces an unpredictable trajectory ("knuckleball" effect). At a critical speed (~12-13 m/s), asymmetrical vortices create random lateral lift forces. This is the serve to master first.
biomechanics: Full kinetic chain: legs → hips → torso → shoulder → elbow → hand
"Bow and arrow" position: elbow high above the shoulder, hand behind the ear
Wrist LOCKED and firm — absolutely required for the float effect
Contact: heel of the hand on the center of the ball
"Punch and freeze": SHORT follow-through — the hand stops immediately after contact
steps: Body at 45° to the net, feet shoulder-width apart
Left arm extended in front of the shoulder, ball at head height
Very short toss: "place" the ball 30-50 cm above the shoulder — the ball does not spin
Left foot steps toward the target right after placing the ball
Full arm extension at contact, hand firm and flat
FREEZE: stop the motion immediately after contact — no arm follow-through

errors.label: Extended follow-through
errors.text: Failure cause #1: follow-through adds spin that kills the float — freeze immediately

errors.label: Toss too high
errors.text: The ball drops into the net — keep the toss short, only 30-50 cm

errors.label: Spinning toss
errors.text: Puts spin on the ball — place the ball, don't toss it

errors.label: Contact with the palm alone
errors.text: Use the heel of the hand (base of the palm) for a flat surface

exercises: Toss & Drop: mark a spot on the floor, toss 20 times without hitting — aim for 18/20 on the mark
"Punch and freeze" against a wall at 3 m: work on stopping the motion instantly
5 consecutive no-spin serves visually validated by a partner

items.name: Jump float serve
items.tagline: jump float — the standard for elite women's volleyball
items.description: Float with a short approach and a jump. Gains contact height, speed, and angle of descent. Has become the standard at elite women's level (86% of serves in pro women according to recent studies). Lower risk than the jump topspin while being more disruptive than the standing float.
biomechanics: Short approach (2 to 4 steps)
Arms in bow-and-arrow position during the jump — different from the spike where the arms drive upward
The approach provides the ball speed, not the arm alone
Contact at the highest point, slightly in front of the head
Locked wrist + freeze identical to the standing float
steps: Position 2-3 m behind the line, ball in the left hand
Step 1 (right) initiates, arms relaxed
Step 2 (left): toss the ball to ~1.5 m height, no rotation
Step 3 + hop: takeoff on both feet behind the line — arms rise into bow-and-arrow
Vertical jump, slightly forward, body braced
Strike with arm extended, heel of the hand on the center of the ball
Immediate FREEZE — land inside the court

errors.label: Toss too high
errors.text: Jump spin reflex — keep the toss short, like the standing float

errors.label: Arms swinging like in a spike
errors.text: Turns into a spin serve — maintain the bow-and-arrow position

errors.label: Extended follow-through
errors.text: Same as the standing float: freeze is mandatory

errors.label: Foot fault at takeoff
errors.text: Make sure the takeoff is behind the end line

exercises: Master the standing float (solid freeze) before adding the approach
Approach only without hitting: work on a stable, low toss
Jump float at controlled speed: consistency before power

items.name: Jump topspin serve
items.tagline: jump serve — a spike from behind the line
items.description: "A spike from behind the end line": ball struck at full speed with topspin (50-60 mph in strong clubs). Highest ace potential but also the highest error rate. Reserved for those who have invested 1000+ reps in training.
biomechanics: 3-4 step approach identical to a back-row spike
High toss (1-1.5 m in front of you) with slight forward spin
Sequential rotation: hips → torso → shoulder → elbow → wrist
Contact in the 10-11 o'clock zone of the ball
Full wrist snap for topspin (~30 rotations/s at elite level)
Full follow-through — opposite of the float
steps: Position 3-4 m behind the line, ball in the hitting hand
Step 1 (right) + high toss with slight induced topspin
Step 2 (left): acceleration
Step 3 (right): long power step, center of gravity dropping
Step 4 (left): takeoff, arms swinging upward
Explosive vertical-forward jump
Strike at the top: hand passes over the ball (10 o'clock), palm then fingers rolling over
Full wrist snap + follow-through — land 1-2 m inside the court

errors.label: Toss too low or behind you
errors.text: Net fault cause #1 — the toss must be high and in front

errors.label: Toss too far in front
errors.text: Foot fault — respect the limits of the service zone

errors.label: No wrist snap
errors.text: The ball sails long without descending spin

errors.label: Using it in matches without prep
errors.text: 1000 reps in training first — golden rule

exercises: Golden rule: 1000 reps in training before using it in a match
"Control" jump spin: lower toss, reduced speed, aim at specific zones
Film your toss: 80% of errors come from toss placement

rows.effect: Blocks the setter release in a 5-1 system
Disrupts the right-side start, excludes the libero
Blocks the middle, breaks up quick attacks
Forces the main hitter to pass AND attack

tips.label: Seams
tips.text: Aiming at the space between two passers is more effective than aiming at a player — it stresses the opponent's communication.

tips.label: Alternate short/long
tips.text: Prevents the setter from knowing when to back off. The short float (zones 2-3-4) behind the attack line is particularly disruptive.

tips.label: FBSO% metric
tips.text: A serve that drops the opponent's First Ball Side Out from 70% to 45% without producing an ace is a very effective serve.

learningHierarchy.label: ★ LEARNING HIERARCHY
learningHierarchy.footer: Master each level before moving on to the next. Consistency beats power.

goldenRule.body: Passing determines 60% of a team's offensive success. Without a good reception, no quick attack. The platform is passive — the legs are active.

format.title: Game format
format.description: The reception systems, the setter's role and the common errors below adapt to the chosen format.

readyPosition.title: Ready position
points: Feet slightly wider than shoulders, one foot slightly forward
Knees flexed toward the inside of the feet, hips low, torso angled at 30-45°
Back straight, weight on the balls of the feet (heels slightly light but not lifted)
Arms SEPARATED (not joined), bent at 90-145°, at waist height
Eyes on the server from the toss
readyPosition.errorText: having arms already joined into a platform before the ball arrives — it slows down movement and prevents the late choice between bump and hands.

tips.title: Sweet spot
tips.text: The ideal contact surface is between 2.5 and 15 cm above the wrists.

tips.title: Cup and fold
tips.text: Recommended technique: one closed fist, the other hand wraps over the top — thumbs parallel and pointing down.

tips.title: Thumbs down
tips.text: Pointing the thumbs toward the floor rotates the forearms outward and tightens the platform.

tips.title: Never interlace
tips.text: NEVER interlace fingers on a powerful serve — risk of fracture.

tips.title: Angle is everything
tips.text: "The ball goes where the platform looks" — for a deep pass: platform at 45°; for a short pass: platform more parallel to the floor.

steps.title: Execution — key steps
items: Read the server: identify the serve type before contact.
Ready position with arms separated (NOT joined in advance).
Read the trajectory from the moment of the opponent's contact.
Move (shuffle steps), arrive BEHIND the ball before the arms come together.
Build the platform early: join the hands when the ball arrives, not too soon.
FREEZE: stop completely just before contact, weight on the front foot — hold for 1-2 seconds.
Contact on the sweet spot, shoulders oriented toward the target setter.
Follow-through: hips and shoulders move toward the target — no arm swing.
steps.freezeText: "Pose for a picture" — freeze completely 1-2 seconds after contact. At 50-90 km/h, a defender in motion cannot adjust their angle. Still, they can move in any direction.

items.name: Lateral (shuffle steps)
items.desc: The foot on the ball side leaves first. Shuffle without crossing, hips low. Arrive behind the ball, reorient toward the target, freeze + platform at the last moment. For longer distances: cross-over step, then pivot.

items.name: Forward (short ball)
items.desc: For short serves or tips. Often ends in a forward lunge: knee collapses toward the floor, platform placed in front of the front knee.

items.name: Backward (drop step)
items.desc: Pivot the foot then shuffle backward. NEVER run backward (loss of balance). If too late to back up: pivot and create a platform off to the side.

oneHand.label: One-arm pass — emergency
oneHand.text: Last-resort technique when the ball is too far for two arms. Arm extended, flat platform on the inner forearm, no swing — just a stab to deflect upward. Variants: one-arm stab (fist on a hard-driven ball), one-arm scoop (open palm up, ball low).

systems.alert5: Indoor 5v5 has no dedicated FIVB or FFVb rulebook. The systems below are logical adaptations of the 6v6 5-1 documented by VolleyballXL, The Art of Coaching Volleyball and Volleyball Canada.
systems.alert4: Indoor 4v4 has no official FIVB rulebook. The formations below come from university intramurals (USA), FFVb / Volleyball Canada coaching manuals, and the beach literature (Brandon Joyner, Better at Beach).

6.name: W system — 5 passers
6.desc: 3 players in the front line, 2 in the back — everyone except the setter participates. Historical formation that gives its name to the "W-formation" (FIVB, USAV IMPACT).
pros: Smaller zones per player (~1.8 m lane)
Ideal for volleyball schools and U13-U15
cons: Many overlap zones between 5 players
Weaker passers forced to participate
Disorganizes attackers (3 front-row players in reception)

6.name: U system — 3 passers
6.desc: Libero in zone 6 (main target of servers), outsides in zones 5 and 1. The 3 best passers take all the balls, all front-row attackers release.
pros: Front-row attackers free for their approach
cons: Wider side lanes to cover (~3 m per player)
Requires a high-performing libero
Vulnerable to short serves in the corners

6.name: 2-passer reception — libero + R4
6.desc: Only 2 passers (libero + a selected R4) cover the full width. Used at high levels to free the 2nd R4 and let them prepare to attack without reception fatigue.
pros: All attackers available for the offensive transition
Stronger block/attack because attackers aren't worn down by reception
Preferred system for pro teams (Poland, France, Italy)
cons: Requires 2 highly athletic passers (~4.5 m lane each)
No margin for error — a poorly read serve = point for the opponent
Unusable without an international-level libero

5.name: 3-passer reception — 2F-3B setup
5.desc: The 3 back-row players (P5, P6, P1) pass. The setter in P1 releases from reception and penetrates the moment the server contacts the ball, like in 6v6 5-1. The 2 front-row players (P4, P3) are free for their approach.
cons: 3 passers across 9 m (~3 m per player)
The setter must read fast and decide to penetrate in < 1 second
Hole in P1 if the setter leaves too early

5.name: 4-passer reception — 3F-2B setup
5.desc: The 2 back-row players (P5, P1) + 2 front-row players (typically P4 and P3 — the setter in P2 releases) pass. The setter stays at the target: no penetration, immediate distribution.
pros: Ideal for mixed or beginner teams
Setter already at the target — no transition
cons: Only 2 front-row attackers available (P4 + P3 or P4 + middle)
Front-row passers then have to run their approach
Double block hard since the setter goes up to the net

5.name: Pentagon reception — 4 or 5 players
5.desc: 5 passers (equivalent to the W with 5 players). 1 player at the front middle (often a dedicated setter), the 2 outsides at midcourt, the 2 back-row players deep. Everyone passes unless the middle player is a dedicated setter.
cons: Lots of overlaps with 5 players
No attacker is released
Ineffective as the level rises

4.name: Diamond (3 passers)
4.desc: Setter at the front middle (P3, released from reception). The 2 outsides (P4, P2) at midcourt + the lone back-row player (P1) deep do the passing. The most widely used formation in indoor 4v4 (university intramurals).
pros: Setter already at the target — no penetration
cons: Covering 9 m of width with 3 = ~3 m per player
The lone back-row player must defend the entire back after the pass
Only 2 front-row attackers

4.name: Line 3-1 (3 passers)
4.desc: Lone setter in P1 (back row) who penetrates the moment the opponent's serve makes contact, heading toward zone 2. The 3 front-row players (P4, P3, P2) pass. Simplified equivalent of the 6v6 5-1.
pros: The setter can also attack after distribution
cons: Requires very clean reception (penetration is unforgiving)
Hole in P1 if the setter leaves before the ball is defended
All attackers have to know how to pass

4.name: Box 2-2 (4 passers)
4.desc: 2 front-row players (P4, P2) + 2 back-row players (P5, P1), no dedicated setter at the net. The best-placed player makes the 2nd touch. Typical of introductory sessions or U11-U13.
pros: Covers the entire court (4 zones of 2.25 m)
No technical demand on the setter
cons: No dedicated setter — random distribution
No attacker is released for their approach
Ineffective as the level rises

6.title: BACK-ROW setter (P1 / P6 / P5) — 5-1 rotations P1, P6, P5
bullets: Releases from reception: no ball is intended for them.
Starts in a special position (e.g. P1: ~7.5 m from the net, 1 m from the right line), hidden behind another player (stack).
Penetrates toward the target (between Z2 and Z3, ~1 m from the net, 3 m right of center) THE MOMENT the opposing serve makes contact — not before (overlap fault).
P1: shortest penetration; P6: central penetration; P5: longest (diagonal) penetration.
3 front-row attackers available (R4 + middle + opposite) + back-row attacks.

6.title: FRONT-ROW setter (P2 / P3 / P4) — 5-1 rotations P2, P3, P4
bullets: Releases from reception: already near the target.
In P2: already at the target — also becomes the line blocker against the opponent's Z4 outside (double defensive load).
In P3: lateral switch to the target immediately after the serve contact.
In P4: crosses the entire net to reach the target (the longest front-row movement).
Only 2 front-row attackers (offset by a pipe from P6 and a back-row attack from the opposite in P1).

5.title: PENETRATING setter (2F-3B setup, recommended)
bullets: Starts in P1 back row, releases from reception.
Penetrates toward the target (Z2/Z3, ~1 m from the net) THE MOMENT the opposing serve makes contact — same as 6v6 5-1.
The 3 back-row players (P5 + P6 + P1 leaving) handle the 3-passer reception.
Must wait for the ball to be defended before leaving (common error: premature start → hole in P1).
5.note: Setup closest to 6v6 — recommended to prepare for the transition.

5.title: FIXED FRONT-ROW setter (3F-2B or pentagon setup)
bullets: Stays at the target (P2 or P3 depending on setup): no penetration.
Releases from reception: no ball is intended for them.
Immediate distribution as soon as the pass arrives — no transition.
In P2: also becomes the line blocker against the opposing outside hitter (as in 6v6 5-1).

4.title: FRONT-ROW setter in diamond (P3 center net)
bullets: Stays at the target (Z3, ~1 m from the net): no penetration.
Releases from reception: the 3 others (2 outsides + 1 back-row) pass.
Quick distribution to Z4 or Z2 depending on pass quality.
Their defense → set transition has to be done in under 2 seconds (only 1 back-row player = lots of coverage).
4.note: Most widely used formation in indoor 4v4.

4.title: PENETRATING setter in line 3-1 (P1 back row)
bullets: Starts in P1 back row, releases from reception.
Penetrates toward zone 2 as soon as the opposing serve makes contact.
The 3 front-row players (P4, P3, P2) pass.
Requires very clean reception — otherwise the setter can't reach the target in time.

4.title: No dedicated setter (box 2-2)
bullets: The best-placed player after the 1st touch makes the 2nd touch.
Everyone passes — 4 zones of ~2.25 m.
Random distribution to one of the 3 other players.
Reserved for introductory sessions (U11-U13, school).

6.title: The libero — keystone of reception in 6v6
6.text: Defensive specialist in a contrasting jersey. Systematically replaces the middles when they rotate to the back row (unlimited substitutions, not counted under FIVB Rule 19). Plays 3 consecutive rotations in Z5-Z6-Z1. Preferred reception position: Z6 (main target of servers) or Z5. FIVB restrictions: no block, no attack above the net, no overhand set in front of the 3 m line if a teammate then attacks above the net.

5.title: No official libero in 5v5
5.text: Indoor 5v5 has no FIVB rulebook. In practice, no federation authorizes a libero in this format. The best passer is placed in P6 or P5 and systematically plays the back row — they become the "de facto libero" without the contrasting jersey or the restrictions. So they can block and attack if needed.

4.title: No libero in 4v4
4.text: No libero is authorized in 4v4 rules (university intramurals, FFVb coaching, beach 4s). The lone back-row player in the diamond — or the penetrating setter in line 3-1 — takes on the role of best passer/defender. With ~3 m of lane per passer in the diamond, anticipation matters more than technique.

reading.title: Reading the serve to position yourself

rows.adapt: Normal position, take the ball high
Upright position, move forward to take it early before it deviates
Low position, ready to back up, angled platform
Can be taken with an overhand set 4 m from the net
Low position, anticipate backing up, rigid passive platform
Platform ready for both scenarios (float or topspin)

cues: Server's position on the line → preferred angle
Height and placement of the toss: high+behind → topspin; low+in front → float
Approach length: long → jump topspin; short → jump float
Direction of the server's shoulders at contact → direction of the ball

common.label: Swinging arms
common.text: Cause #1 — arms swinging at contact, unpredictable ball. Fix: "the platform is passive, the legs are active".

common.label: Broken platform
common.text: One forearm higher than the other — lock the elbows and push the thumbs down.

common.label: Arms joined too early
common.text: Slows movement and prevents the late bump/hands choice. Join the hands only on arrival.

common.label: Torso too upright
common.text: The platform passes under the ball → pass too far from the net. Lean forward 30-45°.

common.label: Contact above the navel
common.text: Too high = reduced control. Aim for contact at waist height or lower.

common.label: No freeze
common.text: Still moving at contact = direction impossible to control. Freeze completely.

6.label: Libero out of position
6.text: Too centered, they miss short serves in the corners; too lateral, they give up the middle. Reference target: Z6 lined up with the opposing server.

6.label: Setter overlap
6.text: The setter leaves their position before the opposing serve contact — fault #1 in 5-1 (FIVB Rule 7.4). Their feet must respect front/back relationships until contact.

6.label: 5-passer reception with no clear roles
6.text: In the W, the 3 front-row players get in each other's way in the middle zone. Explicitly define who takes the ball between P3 and P6 on axial serves.

5.label: Setter leaving too early
5.text: In 2F-3B setup with a penetrating setter, leaving before the ball is defended = hole in P1. Wait for confirmation.

5.label: 2 passers side by side
5.text: In 3F-2B setup, P5 and P1 must be spaced (one per side) and not centered together. Otherwise, the sidelines are uncovered.

5.label: Front-row passer forgetting to attack
5.text: In 3F-2B setup, the front-row player who passes then has to run their attack approach — a reflex to drill specifically.

5.label: No de facto libero defined
5.text: Without a clear role, the 3 back-row players defer to each other. Explicitly designate the best passer as the priority in the central zone.

4.label: Diamond setter who passes
4.text: In the diamond, the setter in P3 must RELEASE from reception — otherwise they can't distribute quickly. The 3 others take it.

4.label: Lone back-row player overloaded
4.text: In the diamond, the back-row P1 covers ~3.5 m of backcourt alone. Anticipation = skill #1; constant shuffling and early reading.

4.label: Box 2-2 with no call on 2nd touch
4.text: Without a dedicated setter, who sets? Shouting "MINE!" on the 2nd touch right after reception is non-negotiable.

4.label: Diamond outsides in a straight line
4.text: P4 and P2 at midcourt at the same depth as P1 → the short cut shot drops between them. Stagger the positions.

zone4.label: Position 2 (opposite / OPP)
zone4.text: Line blocker — blocks, goes up to the net on the right side.

zone4.label: Position 3 (middle)

zone4.label: Position 5 (Libero)

zone3.label: Position 3 (middle)
zone3.text: Solo block in read or commit depending on opponent scouting.

zone3.label: Positions 4 and 2 (outsides)
zone3.text: On the attack line (~2-2.5 m from the net, 0.5 m from the sidelines): cover block deflections and balls through the block.

zone3.label: Position 5 (Libero)
zone3.text: Facing the middle attacker, in their hitting lane (~7-8 m from the net).

zone3.label: Position 6 (back middle)
zone3.text: Shoulders facing the attacker; defends the hard ball through the block (axis ~8-8.5 m).

zone3.label: Position 1 (back right)

zone3.label: Key rule

zone2.label: Position 4 (R4)

zone2.label: Position 3 (middle)

zone2.label: Position 2 (opposite / OPP)

zone2.label: Position 5 (Libero)
zone2.text: Defends the deep line in the block shadow, ~7-7.5 m from the net, 0.5 m from the left line.

zone2.label: Position 6 (back middle)

zone2.label: Position 1 (setter or OH/OPP)
zone2.text: Defends the long deep cross-court, ~7-8 m from the net.

zone4: Opposing Z4 attack (opponent's left wing) → ball arrives on our right.
2-1-2 system: double block (P2 opposite line + P3 cross) + 2 deep defenders.
P4 (left outside) as off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net, 1 m from the line — covers tip and cut shot.
P5 (~7-7.5 m, 0.5 m from left line) defends the long deep cross-court.
P1 (~7-7.5 m, 0.5 m from right line) defends the deep line in the block shadow.
Main shot defended: long deep cross-court (statistically the most frequent trajectory).
zone3: Quick middle attack (Z3) — short angles, little reaction time.
Solo block: P3 (middle) reading, no commit possible.
P4 and P2 (off-blockers) at 2 m from the net on the attack line — cover deflections.
P5 and P1 moved up 1 m (~7 m from the net) — shorter angles than on a high ball.
Weakness: no dedicated central deep defender (only 2 back-row players in 5v5).
Key rule: "stopped on contact" — everyone stopped and balanced at the moment of contact.
zone2: Opposing Z2 attack (opponent's right wing) → ball arrives on our left. Perfect mirror of Z4.
Double block: P4 (R4 line) + P3 (middle cross).
P2 (opposite / setter) as off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net on the right side.
P1 (~7-7.5 m, 1 m from right line) defends the long deep cross.
P5 (~7-7.5 m, 0.5 m from left line) defends the deep line in the block shadow.

zone4: Opposing Z4 attack → ball arrives on our right side.
3F-2B configuration: 3 front-row players → favorable double block (P3 + P2 setter-blocker).
P4 (R4) short off-blocker on the left on the attack line (~2-2.5 m from the net).
P5 defends the long deep cross-court (~7 m, 0.5 m from left line).
P1 defends the deep right line in the block shadow (~7 m, 0.5 m from right line).
Drawback: only 2 deep defenders → 30+ m² per defender (vs 20 m² in 6v6).
zone3: Quick middle attack (Z3) — short angles.
With 3 front-row players, a triple block is possible but leaves only 2 floor defenders — not recommended.
Recommended: double block (P3 + the outside closest to the hitting lane).
P5 and P1 moved up 1 m (~7 m) because angles are shorter on a quick.
Weakness: deep axial ball uncovered (no Z6 defender in 5v5 3F-2B).
zone2: Opposing Z2 attack → ball arrives on our left side. Perfect mirror of Z4.
Double block: P4 (R4 line) + P3 (middle cross).
The setter (P2) as off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net on the right (anti-tip + fast transition to the target).
P1 defends the long deep cross (~7-7.5 m).
P5 defends the deep left line in the block shadow.

zone4: Opposing Z4 attack → ball arrives on our right.
2F-3B configuration (P4+P3 front, P5+P6+P1 back, P1 penetrating): solo block.
P3 (middle) blocks alone on the right side — no P2 available for a double block.
P4 (R4) off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net on the left side.
3 deep defenders: P5 long cross, P6 central axis (~7-8 m), P1 right line.
The 1-1-3 system (1 blocker + 1 off-blocker + 3 defenders) is the closest defense to 6v6 perimeter.
zone3: Quick middle attack (Z3) — short angles.
Solo block (P3) reading — the quick is the hardest target in 2F-3B.
P4 shifted laterally midcourt (~2 m from the net) for deflections.
Advantage: 3 deep defenders (P5, P6, P1) cover the 3 main back zones.
P6 faces the middle attacker in their hitting lane (~7.5-8 m, axis).
zone2: Opposing Z2 attack → ball arrives on our left. Mirror of Z4.
Solo block: P4 blocks alone on the left side (no P2 in 2F-3B).
P3 (middle) becomes the off-blocker on the right side at 2-2.5 m from the net.
P5 defends the deep left line, P6 the axis, P1 the long deep cross.

zone4: Opposing Z4 attack → ball arrives on our right side.
Diamond formation (1-2-1) → system A: 1 blocker (P3) + 3 defenders.
P3 goes up to a solo block on the right side (facing the opposing hitter).
P2 (front right) drops back to the 3 m line at 3.5-4 m from the net — covers tip and tips behind the block.
P4 (front left) drops back to midcourt on the left side — covers the short cross.
P1 (lone back-row) defends the long deep cross (~7-7.5 m, 1 m from right line).
Anticipation = skill #1: only 1 back-row player → ~40 m² to cover.
zone3: Quick middle attack (Z3) — the hardest setup in 4v4: little time, only 1 blocker.
Solo block (P3 alone) in permanent READ mode (no commit possible).
P4 and P2 drop back to midcourt (~3.5-4 m from the net, cover both short crosses).
The lone back-row P1 acts as the Z6 defender (central axis, 7-8 m from the net).
Main shot: hard axial ball (toward P1) since the solo block only covers the middle.
zone2: Opposing Z2 attack → ball arrives on our left side. Perfect mirror of Z4.
System A: 1 blocker (P3) + 3 defenders.
P4 (front left) drops back to the 3 m line at 3.5-4 m — covers tip and tips on the left side.
P2 (front right) drops back to midcourt on the right side — covers the short cross.
The lone back-row P1 defends the long deep cross (~7-7.5 m, 1 m from left line).

zone4: Opposing Z4 attack → ball arrives on our right side.
Box formation (2-2 / box) → system A: 1 blocker (P2) + 3 defenders.
P2 (front right) solo block facing the opposing hitter, takes the line.
P4 (front left) as off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net — covers tip and cut shot on the left side.
P5 defends the long deep cross (~7 m, 0.5 m from left line).
P1 defends the deep line / short cross (~7 m, in the block shadow).
System B (double block P2+P4) is possible but leaves only 2 defenders — reserve for big hitters.
zone3: Quick middle attack (Z3) — short angles, little time.
Double block (P4 + P2) closes the middle — system B with 2 defenders behind.
P5 and P1 take the short crosses (~7 m, 0.5-1 m from the lines).
Major weakness: no short coverage behind the block — the box has no midcourt player.
Alternative: solo block (P3-like role, here P4 or P2 alone) to free a tip defender.
zone2: Opposing Z2 attack → ball arrives on our left side. Perfect mirror of Z4.
System A: 1 blocker (P4) + 3 defenders.
P4 (front left) solo block facing the opposing hitter, takes the line.
P2 (front-right setter-attacker) as off-blocker at 2-2.5 m from the net — anti-tip + fast transition to the target.
P1 defends the long deep cross (~7 m, 0.5 m from right line).
P5 defends the short deep line (~7 m, in the block shadow).

universalsCard.title: ★ Universal defensive principles (4v4 / 5v5 / 6v6)
universalsCard.intro: These principles drawn from Hebert, Liskevych and Volleyball Canada apply regardless of the number of players on the court.
items: Back-row defenders position based on the block's shadow and orientation — not independently.
Stopped and balanced at the moment of contact
Any defender still moving when the hitter swings sees their reactivity collapse ("stopped on contact").
"Ball → opposing setter → ball → opposing hitter". In 4v4 and 5v5, the player deficit demands an even earlier read.
Even in recreational play, the blocker must call "line" or "cross" — without it, the back-row defenders don't know what to cover.
Someone has to cover the 3-5 m behind the block — it's the most neglected zone in smaller formats (4v4 / 5v5).
The setter must never leave for the target before confirming the ball is defended ("release call").

readingAttacker.title: 4. Reading the attacker: visual cues
readingAttacker.intro: Your positioning has to adjust based on what you see. Here are the key cues:

indicators.title: Attacker far from the net
points: High risk of tip or off-speed

indicators.title: Attacker close to the net
points: Set less than 1 m from the net
Back up as far as possible

indicators.title: The attacker's shoulder
points: Shoulder high and back = hard spike
Shoulder rotation = direction of the ball

readingAttacker.proTipText: In the first 2 seconds after the opposing serve, focus your eyes on the setter, then IMMEDIATELY on the attacker about to swing.

advanceRetreat.title: 5. When to move up or back?
advanceRetreat.label: Quick decision tree

advance.title: Move up (3–4 m from the net) when:
items: You are on the same side as the attacker
The attacker is far from the net (bad pass)
You anticipate a tip or off-speed
The block is solid — fewer hard balls get through

retreat.title: Move back (6–7 m from the net) when:
items: You are on the opposite side from the attacker
The attacker has a good pass close to the net
The attacker is powerful or tall

6.title: The ten common defensive positioning mistakes
6.intro: Typology drawn from Mike Hebert (Thinking Volleyball), John Forman (CoachingVB), USA Volleyball and the FIVB Top Volley manual.
mistakes: 1. Drifting into the block shadow

Defenders instinctively take shelter behind the blockers instead of positioning around the block shadow — leaving the cross-courts and off-the-block trajectories open. Hebert: "creeping into the block shadow".
2. Faulty reading

The defender locks onto the ball instead of following the sequence "ball → setter → ball → hitter". Result: they guess instead of reading, and aren't stopped or balanced at the moment of contact ("stopped and balanced at the moment of contact").
3. Libero out of depth

Too close to the net, they can't defend deep spikes; too far, they miss the tips. Rule: line up your outside shoulder with the inside shoulder of the middle blocker, 6-8 m from the net depending on the block.
4. Defending setter unprepared
Stance too low or oriented wrong, preventing them from seeing ball + opposing court; premature start toward the target creating a Z1 hole; no "release call" signaling they're leaving the defense.
5. Overlap faults

Most common: Z6 drifts in front of Z3, Z5 ends up right of Z6, and the setter leaves too early to penetrate (fault #1 in 5-1). At the instant the server contacts the ball, every foot must respect front/back and left/right relationships (Rule 7.4).
6. Forgotten reception → defense transition

Players stay frozen in their W reception formation instead of shifting into base defensive position the moment the opposing setter touches the ball. Hebert: "sluggish recovery after play on the ball".
7. Bad zone 6 management

Confusion between "6-up" (rotation), "6-back" (perimeter) and "6-deep". The Z6 player must shift laterally based on the opposing attack side, not stay centered. Leaning back to dig puts the weight on the heels and kills reactivity.
8. Failed defense against the quick

Reading the opposing middle too late; back-row not moved up (on a quick, Z1 and Z5 must gain a meter toward the net because angles are shorter); "false stepping" (first step backward) loses available time.
9. Orphaned tip coverage

No defender explicitly assigned to the tip; "standing up on tips" — the defender is low for the spike, then stands up and extends their hands on the tip, letting the ball drop right in front of them. Focus must stay on the spike in a low stance, with a tip jump available.
10. Collective silence
No calls ("tip!", "line!", "out!", "mine!"); blockers who don't communicate their line vs cross orientation; no rotation captain checking overlaps before the serve.

5.title: Common errors in 5v5
5.intro: Errors specific to the 5v5 format (adaptations from the Volleyball Canada doc, VolleyballXL, and 6v6 doctrine).
mistakes: 1. Mechanically copying 6v6
Covering 3 deep zones with 3 defenders works (2F-3B setup), but the off-blocker who pulls back is missing — the 3 m zone isn't covered if no one is explicitly assigned.
2. The off-blocker stuck at the net
After the block, the off-blocker has to pull back to 2-2.5 m to cover tips. If they stay at the net, the zone behind the block is wide open.
3. 2 defenders standing side by side
In 3F-2B setup, the 2 deep defenders must be spread (one left side, one right side), not centered together. Otherwise, the sidelines are uncovered.
4. Setter leaves too early (penetrating setup)
In 2F-3B setup with a penetrating setter from P1, they have to wait for the ball to be defended before running to the target — otherwise hole in Z1.
5. Front/back confusion

With 5 players, the temptation is to let the front-row players defend their side by staying on the 3 m line — but that leaves the back open. Front-row players go up to the block, back-row players defend deep.
6. Faulty reading
The one-player deficit demands an even earlier read than in 6v6. "Ball → setter → ball → hitter" sequence + balanced stop at contact.

4.title: Common errors in 4v4
4.intro: Errors specific to indoor 4v4 (university intramurals, FFVb / Volleyball Canada doctrine, beach 4s).
mistakes: 1. Isolated blocker with no tip coverage
The 3 defenders all go deep, leaving the 3-5 m zone empty. Someone has to always be assigned to the tip at 3.5-4 m from the net.
2. 2 defenders in a straight line
Side by side at the same depth → the cut shot drops between them. In 4v4, defenders must always be staggered (one close, one far) or spread laterally.
3. The setter running to set before the ball is defended
Premature transition leaves a defensive hole. The setter waits for confirmation that the ball is up before leaving for the target.
4. No signal between blocker and defenders
The blocker MUST call "line" or "cross" before the attack starts. Otherwise, the 3 defenders don't know what to cover — everyone improvises.
5. Tip defender too far from the net
They back up with the other back-row players and can no longer cover short tips. Their position is 3.5-4 m from the net, in the axis — not 7 m.
6. "Random" block by the wrong player
In 4v4, blocking with a poorly placed player (far from the hitter) leaves the opponent facing 3 misaligned defenders. The blocker has to be the one in front of the main hitter.
7. Faulty reading
With ~40 m² per defender (vs 20 m² in 6v6), a reading error is unrecoverable. Anticipation = skill #1 in 4v4.

serviceTransition.title: 7. Positioning at the serve
serviceTransition.intro: Your serve position is DIFFERENT from your defensive position. The moment the serve leaves, you need to reposition.
steps: Your team serves
You're in rotation position
The server hits
You watch the opposing setter
The setter touches the ball
You move toward your defensive zone
The hitter jumps
You're in your final position, ready to react

communication.title: 8. Defensive communication
communication.intro: A silent defense is an ineffective defense.

calls: Calls out the zone the attack is coming from
If the block doesn't cover the line
You take the ball (the MOST important)
You leave the ball for a teammate
The ball is going out, don't touch it
We keep the defense in place

communication.ruleText: In doubt between two players, it's ALWAYS the player further forward who takes the ball.

6.title: The three major defensive systems (FIVB / USAV)

warning.label: ⚠ Terminology warning
warning.text: The expression "W defense" often heard in France is incorrect. The "W-formation" historically refers to a 5-passer service reception formation — not a defensive system. International doctrine (FIVB, USAV IMPACT, Liskevych, Stone) distinguishes three systems: man-up (2-1-3), perimeter (2-0-4) and rotational (3-2-1).

systems.name: Man-up defense (2-1-3)
systems.principe: A defender moves up to the 3 m line behind the block to intercept tips and off-speeds. Two blockers at the net, the off-blocker pulls back, and three deep players cover the long angles.
forces: Outstanding coverage of tips, roll shots and "junk" balls behind the block
Fast transition to attack if the player who came up is the setter
Simple to teach to young teams
faiblesses: Only 3 deep defenders — vulnerable to hard sharp cross-courts
A hitter who swings hard between the blockers gets through easily
systems.indication: Young teams, school teams, tactical opponents who use a lot of tips or off-speed.

systems.name: Perimeter defense (2-0-4)
systems.tag: White defense — dominant system at high-level men's volleyball
systems.principe: The four back-row defenders form a U open toward the net, almost on the sidelines and end line — "one foot on the line" (Liskevych). The middle of the court is intentionally given up.
forces: Excellent coverage of hard spikes, lines, and deep corners
Simple collective movement
Dominant system in modern international men's volleyball
faiblesses: Very vulnerable to short tips behind the block — central zone between 3 and 5 m open
Requires athletic defenders capable of diving forward
systems.indication: Senior, men's, international level, powerful opponents.

systems.name: Rotational defense (3-2-1)
systems.principe: The three back-row defenders slide toward the opposing attack side: the opposite back-row player moves up behind the block (tip), the middle slides toward the attacked line, the defender on the attacked side covers the sharp angle.
forces: Excellent coverage of the deep line AND the tip simultaneously
Highly adaptable system
Fast setter transition when the setter is in P1
faiblesses: One fewer defender deep (one player dedicated to the tip)
Opposite diagonal corner vulnerable
Requires strong reading and coordination
systems.indication: Opponents who mix power and lines/tips; intermediate to elite level.

footer.strong: The choice is not about orthodoxy:
footer.text: it depends on the opponent's offensive profile and your defenders' qualities. Modern defense is defined less by the formation than by reading — visual sequence "ball → setter → ball → hitter" and balanced stop at the moment of contact.

warning.label: ⚠ Format not FIVB-official
warning.text: Indoor 5v5 has no dedicated FIVB or FFVb rulebook. These three systems are logical adaptations of 6v6 documented by VolleyballXL, The Art of Coaching Volleyball and Volleyball Canada. There is no official 5v5 technical manual — choose the system based on your team configuration (2-3 or 3-2).

systems.name: 1-1-3 system
systems.principe: Suited to the 2F-3B configuration (2 front, 3 back). The blocker jumps alone; the 2nd front-row player pulls back as off-blocker at 2-3 m from the net for tips; 3 deep defenders cover line, axis, and long cross.
forces: 3 deep defenders like in 6v6 perimeter — good spike coverage
Setup closest to 6v6 5-1 (prep for transition to 6v6)
Tip covered by the off-blocker
faiblesses: Solo block only → fragile against big hitters
The off-blocker at 2-3 m must be very reactive
systems.indication: 2F-3B configuration (penetrating setter), moderately powerful opponents. Recommended system for transitioning to 6v6.

systems.name: 2-1-2 system
systems.principe: Suited to the 3F-2B configuration (3 front, 2 back). Double block at the net, the front middle covers the tip at 2-3 m from the net, 2 deep defenders take the long cross and the line.
forces: Double block like in 6v6 — clearly more effective against hard spikes
3 attackers at the net for the counter-attack
faiblesses: Only 2 deep defenders → 9 m of backcourt very hard to cover
High athletic demand on the 2 back-row players
systems.indication: 3F-2B configuration against very powerful teams. Use at the end of a set when every point counts.

systems.name: 1-2-2 system
systems.principe: Solo blocker + 2 front-zone covers (tip + behind block) + 2 deep defenders. Suited when the opponent uses lots of tips or against beginner teams.
forces: Excellent short-tip coverage (2 front-zone covers)
Tip hard for the opponent to exploit
faiblesses: Only 2 deep defenders → hard spikes are difficult
Requires coordination between the 2 front-zone covers
systems.indication: Opponents who tip a lot; women's volleyball, youth categories, technical teams.

footer.text: the 1-1-3 system in 2F-3B configuration with a penetrating setter is the closest defense to 6v6 — ideal as a pedagogical bridge. The 2-1-2 is only justified against truly powerful hitters.

warning.label: ⚠ Format not FIVB-official
warning.text: Indoor 4v4 has no official FIVB rulebook. These three systems come from university intramurals practice (USA), FFVb / Volleyball Canada transition coaching manuals, and the beach literature (Brandon Joyner, Better at Beach). With 4 players, each defender covers ~30-40 m² (vs 20 m² in 6v6) — anticipation is skill #1.

systems.name: System A: 1 blocker + 3 defenders
systems.principe: A single player goes up to block the main hitter. The 3 others spread out: tip defender (3-4 m from the net, axis), cross defender (7-7.5 m, right line, long cross), line defender (7-7.5 m, in the block shadow).
forces: Covers tip, line, and long cross simultaneously
The most balanced setup in 4v4
Blocker line/cross signal is very effective
faiblesses: Solo block — vulnerable to big hitters
Requires a disciplined tip defender who doesn't back up
systems.indication: Opponents of equivalent or moderate level. The most versatile configuration in 4v4 (diamond or line 3-1).

systems.name: System B: 2 blockers + 2 defenders
systems.principe: Both front-row players go up together against the main hitter. The 2 back-row players take position: one on the line side (7 m, 1 m from the line), one on the axis slightly shifted toward the cross. The tip is uncovered.
forces: Double block clearly more effective against hard spikes
Maximum pressure on the opposing hitter
faiblesses: Only 2 floor defenders → impossible to cover everything
Tip behind the block completely exposed
Forces a choice: line OR cross, not both
systems.indication: Use only against very powerful hitters without finesse (no tips). Box 2-2 or line 3-1 configuration.

systems.name: System C: 0 blockers
systems.principe: No one goes up to block. All 4 players defend deep: 2 at midcourt (3-4 m) for tips, 2 deep (7-8 m) for deeper balls. The setter acts as the 4th defender.
forces: Covers the full depth of the court
Well suited to slow rallies
faiblesses: COUNTERPRODUCTIVE as soon as an opponent swings seriously (the spike goes through unopposed)
No pressure at the net
systems.indication: School level, beginner recreational, opponents who don't spike. To be avoided as soon as the opposition gains power.

footer.text: system A (1 blocker + 3 defenders) is the near-universal default. System B is only justified against truly powerful hitters at the end of a set. System C only works at beginner recreational level — as soon as an opponent spikes, return to system A.

transitions.title: 10. Attack ↔ defense transitions
transitions.intro: Volleyball is a game of fast transitions. You're constantly switching from attack to defense and back.

groups.label: Attack → defense transition
items: Go to your defensive zone (2–3 seconds max)
Bend the legs, ready to dig

groups.label: Defense → attack transition
items: Run to the net to attack or block
Move back slightly, ready to cover the attack
Surround your hitter (in a semicircle at 2–3 m)

items.title: Reading the situation
items.objectif: Learn to identify the attack zone quickly
steps: The coach stands on the other side of the net in zone 4, 3, or 2
You start from the center of the court
The coach calls the zone and tosses the ball
You have to reach your defensive zone in 2–3 seconds
Repeat 20 times varying zones

items.title: Move up/back based on the set
items.objectif: Adjust your position based on set quality
steps: The setter delivers sets of varying quality to the hitter
Set close to the net → back up (hard spike expected)
Set off the net → move up (tip likely)
The hitter swings and you defend
The coach corrects your position after each ball

items.title: Defensive communication
steps: Scrimmage in your format (4v4, 5v5 or 6v6) but SHOUTING every call
Penalty: -1 point if a player doesn't call "Mine!" on their ball
Bonus: +1 point if the whole team communicates on a rally
Every player has to call out the opposing attack zone

items.title: Defense against tips
steps: The hitter ONLY tips and off-speeds
Defenders must all move up (3–4 m)
Goal: dig 8 out of 10 balls
Then alternate: 5 tips, 5 spikes to work on adaptation

items.title: Fast transitions
steps: Normal scrimmage but the coach times the transitions
Goal: be in defensive position in under 3 seconds
If too slow, the team does 5 push-ups and restarts
Gradually increase the rally pace

items.title: Reading the hitter
steps: The hitter alternates spike, tip, and roll without warning
Before they swing, the defender calls their prediction: "Spike!" or "Tip!"
Point if the prediction is correct AND the ball is dug
Focus on: shoulder, approach, position relative to the net

commandments.title: 12. The 10 commandments of the defender
items: Then the hitter, not the ball

conclusion.label: Conclusion
conclusion.body1: Defensive positioning is learned through practice and experience. Don't get discouraged if you make mistakes at first — even pros adjust their placement constantly.
conclusion.body2: The key: apply the base rule (same side = move up, opposite = move back), watch the hitter, communicate with your teammates, and never be afraid to dive for a ball.
